Projects

Automated irrigation controller

Personal project, summer 2026

I built a weatherproof PLC control panel that waters two flower beds from a ground-level rain barrel. It runs the pump automatically when the soil gets dry, and a manual button lets me water on demand. My goal was to build a real industrial-style panel at home scale, from the logic through wiring, commissioning and troubleshooting.

Hardware

Controller
Siemens LOGO! 8.3, programmed in LOGO! Soft Comfort V8.3 using function block diagram
Power
Mean Well MDR-60-24 DIN-rail supply (120 V AC to 24 V DC) on a GFCI-protected outlet
Pump
12 V DC bilge pump, fed from the 24 V bus through a 24 V to 12 V DC-DC converter and switched by a 4-channel 24 V relay module
Sensing
4-wire analog soil moisture sensor (0 to 10 V output) on analog input AI1
Enclosure
IP65 enclosure with a two-rail DIN layout, Allen-Bradley 1492-series terminal blocks and illuminated pushbuttons on the lid
Wiring
14 AWG for 120 V AC, 18 AWG for 24 V DC and 22 AWG shielded for sensor signals, colour coded by voltage

Control logic

The program is split into automatic mode, soil moisture sensing and manual trigger. RS latches hold the automatic and manual toggles, and an analog threshold comparator on AI1 decides when the soil counts as dry. The pump output runs when automatic mode is on and the soil is dry, or when the manual trigger is active. A pulsed output indicates that automatic mode is active. I loaded the program to the PLC over Ethernet, which meant setting up the IP addressing and online settings.

Troubleshooting

During testing one pump channel stayed dead even though its relay LED was lit. I worked through it with a multimeter, checking supply voltage at the relay common and testing the normally open and normally closed contacts with the relay energized, and ruled out my wiring and measurement setup. That traced the fault to a failed channel on the relay module, so I moved the pump to a working channel.

Top mount flywheel launcher

Cornerstone design project, winter 2026. Team of five.

Our team designed and prototyped an autonomous vehicle with a mounted launcher for a simulated search-and-rescue delivery task. The vehicle had to follow a track, stop, and launch three ping-pong balls at a basket 3 m away using mechanically stored energy and an automatic loader, without permanent changes to the robot platform.

My role: I designed the electrical layout, wrote most of the code and designed many of the 3D printed parts.

Design

  • A single vertical flywheel driven by a brushless motor and speed controller stores the energy, and the motor is off during launch.
  • A vertical hopper with a servo-driven V-cradle feeds one ball at a time.
  • Infrared and ultrasonic sensors on an Arduino-based ELEGOO Smart Car V4 handle line following and obstacle avoidance, and the car stops completely before launching.
  • Custom 3D printed PLA parts (flywheel, motor mount, Arduino mount, V-cradle) and PVC pipe for the hopper and barrel, mounted on printed rails that bolt to existing holes so nothing on the car is modified.
  • AutoCAD drawings of the custom parts, a build and wiring procedure, and a cost analysis. Out-of-pocket cost was about $51 CAD, since the motor, battery, servo and kit were already owned.

Results and lessons

Line following and obstacle avoidance worked as designed on the evaluation course, and the autoloader fed balls reliably when tested on its own. During testing the speed controller behaved unpredictably when power-cycled and drove the motor at unsafe speeds. Because that risked a fractured flywheel, we disconnected the motor for the evaluation, so we could not demonstrate live launches.

Our report recommends a controller with programmable limits, a flywheel in PETG or nylon instead of PLA, and proper guarding in line with CCOHS safeguarding guidance. The main lesson was to validate a controller carefully before putting it into a safety-sensitive system. The report also considers the design through the Seventh Generation Principle, covering waste, repairability and battery end of life.
